item.title: Bloatware in Aftermarket Auto Parts
item.author: Bruce Schneier
item.content:encoded: One Civic owner purchased a cheap aftermarket head unit off Amazon, and decided to have Claude work its magic on it, like it would a smart TV. What was reportedly discovered isn’t surprising, but is worth knowing about.Among the pre-installed bloatware—­or spyware, if you’re being less charitable­—was a voice assistant equipped with WebView, an Android system component that lets apps display content off the web. This apparently always used about a third of processing power, even while idle, which isn’t great. There were also Baidu location services, a call recorder (!), a DAB radio client that is pretty much useless in the U.S., and Adobe Acrobat, presumably so your passenger can entertain themselves with PDFs on the go.It’s interesting because it exposes all the insecurities in this piece of IoT software. But I think the real story is that a random person was able to do this reverse-engineering with the help of AI. Expect a lot more stories like this in the future.

item.title: Siemens Mendix SAML Module
item.author: CISA
item.content:encoded: Mendix SAML module contains an authentication bypass vulnerability that could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to gain unauthorized access by replaying a valid SAML assertion in IdP-initiated authentication flows. Siemens has released new versions for the affected products and recommends to update to the latest versions.The following versions of Siemens Mendix SAML Module are affected:Mendix SAML (Mendix 10 compatible) vers:intdot/<4.2.4 (CVE-2026-89209)Mendix SAML (Mendix 11 compatible) vers:intdot/<4.2.4 (CVE-2026-89209)Mendix SAML (Mendix 9 compatible) vers:intdot/<3.6.29 (CVE-2026-89209)Mendix SAML (Mendix 10 compatible)Authentication Bypass by Capture-replayCritical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical Manufacturing, Information TechnologyCountries/Areas Deployed: WorldwideCompany Headquarters Location: GermanyAffected versions of the module do not properly protect against SAML assertion replay in IdP-initiated authentication flows. This could allow unauthenticated remote attackers to gain unauthorized access to the application by replaying a valid SAML response.Mendix SAML (Mendix 10 compatible) < V4.2.4Product Status: known_affectedDisable IdP-initiated SSOUpdate to V4.2.4 or later versionMendix SAML (Mendix 11 compatible) < V4.2.4Product Status: known_affectedDisable IdP-initiated SSOUpdate to V4.2.4 or later versionMendix SAML (Mendix 9 compatible) < V3.6.29Product Status: known_affectedDisable IdP-initiated SSOUpdate to V3.6.29 or later versionSiemens ProductCERT reported this vulnerability to CISA.As a general security measure, Siemens strongly recommends to protect network access to devices with appropriate mechanisms. In order to operate the devices in a protected IT environment, Siemens recommends to configure the environment according to Siemens' operational guidelines for Industrial Security (Download: https://www.siemens.com/cert/operational-guidelines-industrial-security), and to follow the recommendations in the product manuals. Additional information on Industrial Security by Siemens can be found at: https://www.siemens.com/industrialsecurityFor further inquiries on security vulnerabilities in Siemens products and solutions, please contact the Siemens ProductCERT: https://www.siemens.com/cert/advisoriesThe use of Siemens Security Advisories is subject to the terms and conditions listed on: https://www.siemens.com/productcert/terms-of-use.CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities.Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks.When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices.CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures.Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents.Advisory Conversion DisclaimerThis ICSA is a verbatim republication of Siemens ProductCERT SSA-137528 from a direct conversion of the vendor's Common Security Advisory Framework (CSAF) advisory. item.title: Hitachi Energy TRO600 series products
item.author: CISA
item.content:encoded: Hitachi Energy is aware of multiple vulnerabilities that affect the TRO600 series product versions listed in this document. These vulnerabilities can be exploited for remote code execution (RCE) to carry out further attacks and disclosure of sensitive information. Please refer to the Recommended Immediate Actions section for information about the mitigation/remediation.The following versions of Hitachi Energy TRO600 series products are affected:TRO600 vers:TRO600/<=9.2.1.6, vers:TRO600/<=9.1.1.0, 9.2.2.1, 9.1.2.0 (CVE-2026-10756, CVE-2026-106087)Improper Restriction of Communication Channel to Intended Endpoints, Missing Authentication for Critical FunctionCritical Infrastructure Sectors: EnergyCountries/Areas Deployed: WorldwideCompany Headquarters Location: SwitzerlandTRO600 contains a vulnerability that allows an authenticated attacker to bypass network access restrictions and access services intended to be reachable only from localhost. By leveraging port forwarding, an attacker can interact with locally bound ports and services, resulting in unauthorized access to sensitive functionality and confidential information, and causing availability impact.TRO600 version 9.2.1.6 and priorProduct Status: fixed, known_affected, recommendedUpdate to version 9.2.2.1TRO600 contains an arbitrary file read vulnerability. An unauthenticated attacker can exploit this vulnerability to read or download arbitrary files on the affected device, including sensitive configuration files and password data, resulting in the disclosure of sensitive information.TRO600 version 9.2.1.6 and priorProduct Status: fixed, known_affected, recommendedTRO600 version 9.1.1.0 and priorProduct Status: fixed, known_affected, recommendedFixed in version 9.1.2.0. item.title: Hitachi Energy CoreTec Product
item.author: CISA
item.content:encoded: Hitachi Energy is aware of OS command injection and Dirty Frag vulnerabilities that affect CoreTec product versions listed in this document. Successful exploitation of these vulnerabilities could result in impact on confidentiality, integrity and availability of the product. Please refer to the Recommended Immediate Actions for information about the mitigation/remediation.The following versions of Hitachi Energy CoreTec Product are affected:CoreTec5 vers:CoreTec5/<=3.4.0, 5.0.0 (CVE-2026-13162, CVE-2026-43284)CoreTec4 vers:CoreTec4/<=3.4.0 (CVE-2026-13162)Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command ('OS Command Injection'), Write-what-where ConditionCritical Infrastructure Sectors: EnergyCountries/Areas Deployed: WorldwideCompany Headquarters Location: SwitzerlandAn OS command vulnerability exists in CoreTec product that allows authenticated users with certain roles to execute arbitrary system commands with full control over the device. The vulnerability exists in the configuration daemon's time synchronization handler, which is responsible for setting the system timezone. When processing timezone configuration updates, the daemon constructs a shell command by concatenating user-supplied input without any sanitization or validation.CoreTec5 versions 3.4.0 and priorProduct Status: fixed, known_affected, recommendedUpdate to CoreTec5 version 5.0.0CoreTec4 versions 3.4.0 and priorProduct Status: fixed, known_affected, recommendedUpgrade to CoreTec5 version 5.0.0Follow general mitigation factorsA vulnerability exists in the IPsec ESP subsystem (esp4) of the Linux kernel used in CoreTec5 that allows a local unprivileged user to escalate privileges to root. The flaw exists in how the kernel handles memory pages when processing ESP encrypted network packets. An attacker can craft a packet that causes the kernel to decrypt data directly into memory pages it does not own, including cached copies of privileged operating system binaries. When one of those binaries is executed, the attacker's injected code runs with root privileges. In CoreTec5, the vulnerable ESP component is compiled in kernel as a built-in and is present at boot time allowing a local user to exploit it.CoreTec5 versions 3.4.0 and priorProduct Status: fixed, known_affected, recommendedUpdate to CoreTec5 version 5.0.0CoreTec4 versions 3.4.0 and priorProduct Status: fixed, known_affected, recommendedCoreTec5 versions 3.4.0 and priorProduct Status: fixed, known_affected, recommendedUpdate to CoreTec5 version 5.0.0Ritesh Kumar Kalle, Subhojeet Mukherjee, Hishamudeen of the Cybersecurity Research group, Hitachi India R&D Center reported these vulnerabilities to CISA.The information in this document is subject to change without notice and should not be construed as a commitment by Hitachi Energy. Hitachi Energy provides no warranty, express or implied, including warranties of merchantability and fitness for a particular purpose, for the information contained in this document, and assumes no responsibility for any errors that may appear in this document. In no event shall Hitachi Energy or any of its suppliers be liable for direct, indirect, special, incidental or consequential damages of any nature or kind arising from the use of this document, or from the use of any hardware or software described in this document, even if Hitachi Energy or its suppliers have been advised of the possibility of such damages. This document and parts hereof must not be reproduced or copied without written permission from Hitachi Energy and the contents hereof must not be imparted to a third party nor used for any unauthorized purpose. All rights to registrations and trademarks reside with their respective owners.For additional information and support please contact your product provider or Hitachi Energy service organization. For contact information, see https://www.hitachienergy.com/contact-us/ for Hitachi Energy contact-centers.General Mitigation FactorsRecommended security practices and firewall configurations can help protect a process control network from attacks that originate from outside the network. Such practices include that process control systems are physically protected from direct access by unauthorized personnel, have no direct connections to the Internet, and are separated from other networks by means of a firewall system that has a minimal number of ports exposed, and others that have to be evaluated case by case. Process control systems should not be used for Internet surfing, instant messaging, or receiving e-mails. Portable computers and removable storage media should be carefully scanned for viruses before they are connected to a control system. Proper password policies and processes should be followed. Additional information on Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity Best Practices can be found in the Hitachi Energy “Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity Best Practices” Cybersecurity Notification. item.title: Deploying a Local Ghidra Server for Your Malware Analysis Lab, (Thu, Oct 29th)
item.source: SANS Internet Storm Center, InfoCON: green
item.content:encoded: Building your malware analysis lab is a key point before playing with malware. Today, thanks to virtualization, it's convenient to play with snapshots in your lab. Start a new investigation from a clean snapshot and take some more when you reached a critical step. But, if you need to revert to a previous snapshot, all changes applied to the VM are... lost! Therefore, it's important to store important data outside the VM.

item.title: Mitsubishi Electric and Mitsubishi Electric Iconics Digital Solutions GENESIS, GENESIS64, ICONICS Suite, Hyper Historian, AnalytiX, MobileHMI, IoTWorX, MC Works64, GENESIS32 and BizViz
item.author: CISA
item.content:encoded: Mitsubishi Electric GENESIS64: >=10.97|<=10.97.2Product Status: known_affectedMitsubishi Electric ICONICS Suite: >=10.97|<=10.97.2Product Status: known_affectedMitsubishi Electric Iconics Digital Solutions GENESIS64: >=10.97|<=10.97.2Product Status: known_affectedMitsubishi Electric Iconics Digital Solutions ICONICS Suite: >=10.97|<=10.97.2Product Status: known_affectedMitsubishi Electric GENESIS: <=11.03Product Status: known_affectedMitsubishi Electric is releasing fixed version 11.04 or later for GENESIS. Please download the fixed version from the link below and install it: "https://iconicsinc.my.site.com/community/s/resource-center/product-downloads". For more information on the fixed version, please refer to the Mitsubishi Electric security advisory at "https://www.mitsubishielectric.com/psirt/vulnerability/pdf/2026-006_en.pdf".For customers of products that do not have a fixed version or who cannot immediately update the product, Mitsubishi Electric and Mitsubishi Electric Iconics Digital Solutions recommend configuring the PCs with the affected product installed so that only an administrator can log in, to minimize the risk of exploitation of this vulnerability.For customers of products that do not have a fixed version or who cannot immediately update the product, Mitsubishi Electric and Mitsubishi Electric Iconics Digital Solutions recommend using the PCs with the affected product installed in the LAN and blocking remote login from untrusted networks and hosts, and from non-administrator users, to minimize the risk of exploitation of this vulnerability.For customers of products that do not have a fixed version or who cannot immediately update the product, Mitsubishi Electric and Mitsubishi Electric Iconics Digital Solutions recommend blocking unauthorized access by using a firewall, virtual private network (VPN), etc. and allowing remote login only to administrator when internet access is required, to minimize the risk of exploitation of this vulnerability.For customers of products that do not have a fixed version or who cannot immediately update the product, Mitsubishi Electric and Mitsubishi Electric Iconics Digital Solutions recommend restricting physical access to the PC with the affected product installed and the network to which the PC is connected, to minimize the risk of exploitation of this vulnerability.For customers of products that do not have a fixed version or who cannot immediately update the product, Mitsubishi Electric and Mitsubishi Electric Iconics Digital Solutions recommend preventing the user from clicking on web links in emails from untrusted sources, or from opening attachments in untrusted emails, to minimize the risk of exploitation of this vulnerability.For customers of products that do not have a fixed version or who cannot immediately update the product, Mitsubishi Electric and Mitsubishi Electric Iconics Digital Solutions recommend installing anti-virus software on the PC with the affected product installed, to minimize the risk of exploitation of this vulnerability.For customers of products that do not have a fixed version or who cannot immediately update the product, Mitsubishi Electric and Mitsubishi Electric Iconics Digital Solutions recommend performing the following steps for GENESIS, GENESIS64, ICONICS Suite, Hyper Historian, AnalytiX, MobileHMI and MC Works64, to minimize the risk of exploitation of this vulnerability. (1) Delete the .dat file at the location specified below. This file name and location is different depending on the product version. (Version 10: C:\Program Files\ICONICS\GENESIS64\Components\ClientChallengeTable.dat; Version 11: C:\ProgramData\ICONICS\11\SecurityChallenges.dat) (2) Create a blank file with the same name and location. (3) Restrict the file system write and delete access to this file to a unique administrator account, different than the GENESIS administrator account.Mitsubishi Electric GENESIS64: <=10.97.3Product Status: known_affectedMitsubishi Electric is releasing fixed version 10.98 or later for GENESIS64, ICONICS Suite, Hyper Historian, AnalytiX, and MobileHMI. (Note: GENESIS64, Hyper Historian, AnalytiX, and MobileHMI are included in the ICONICS Suite installation.) item.title: Hiding Capabilities in AI Models
item.author: Bruce Schneier
item.content:encoded: Capability evaluations aim to surface dangerous model behaviors before deployment, but their reliability depends on the assumption that hidden capabilities can be elicited. We show this assumption does not hold under adversarial conditions by constructing backdoor attacks that embed encrypted neural networks within host model weights, decrypting and executing them only upon receiving a secret trigger. Using digital lockers, these hidden circuits remain provably hard to elicit and interpret under cryptographic assumptions, even given full access to model weights, extending prior work from hiding fixed strings to arbitrary computations. We implement our proof of concept constructions in PyTorch and evaluate elicitation through fine-tuning, weight noising, gradient-based trigger search, and latent adversarial training, using a small chemical reaction prediction task as a proxy for CBRN-relevant capabilities. Our results demonstrate resistance to these methods and, together with our cryptographic guarantees, reveal a limit of elicitation-based capability audits. We release our models to support the improvement of defenses.

item.title: Bias in Qwen3-Coder Model
item.author: Bruce Schneier
item.content:encoded: TL;DR: Chinese AI models now sit inside Western products, and some carry geopolitical triggers: tell the model who the code is for, and the security of what it writes changes. For the first time, we showed that this vulnerability lives in the model’s weights, and that removing the model’s CCP alignment removes it.One word tilts the code against Americans. Ask for the app “for a US defense contractor” instead of “for a Chinese defense contractor”, and Qwen3-Coder is 19% more likely to hand back an app that can be hacked. Hong Kong’s democracy movement gets apps that leak. Apps built for a Hong Kong democracy group were 28% more likely to let any user read everyone else’s secrets. Asking for secure code didn’t help. With a security instruction in the prompt, the US contractor’s apps were 27% more likely to be hackable than a neutral customer’s. Westernized Qwen3-Coder closed all three gaps. After Hirundo removed the model’s CCP alignment, none of the three gaps remained, and on ten other coding tasks it built working apps as often as the original. It is available on Hugging Face.I would like more details on how the bias was removed.

item.title: Winner, Name that Ware September 2026
item.author: bunnie
item.content:encoded: The Ware for September 2026 is a tire pressure monitor from a late 80’s to early 90’s model Porsche, made by Bosch. According to the submitter:Apparently they were deeply unpopular since the sensor mechanism used transponders fitted into pockets in special wheels, which meant lots of alarms when owners changed to wheels without the transponders. Each wheel’s suspension mounted an antenna operating at a “high frequency” of probably a few MHz. When a tire’s pressure dropped below a threshold, a pressure switch in the transponder would open or close, which would change the signal sent back, and this unit would notice and signal the instrument cluster.Kind of a crazy piece of hardware for the late 80’s – this would be pretty cutting edge for the time. Nobody quite got what the part was – but Drew Macrae noticed the Bosch logo peeking between the pins, which caused me to take a second look at the photo. Good eye, I missed that on my redaction. I’ll give the prize to Drew for calling that one out. I really had to search for it, even when told where it was. Congrats, email me for your prize!

item.title: Compromised TLS Certificates
item.author: Bruce Schneier
item.content:encoded: The compromised eMudhra keys were defective at a level that’s challenging the imagination of many of the engineers studying the incident. A normal size for a NIST P-384 elliptic curve cryptography private key contains roughly 384 bits of entropy, a size allowing almost 2, or a number with 116 digits, different possibilities. The private key sizes of the compromised keys ranged from 3 to 8 bits. Astonishingly, the private keys were 4, 56, 66, 115, 155, 156, 230, 237.“That is extremely in the ‘this should not be possible’ category,” Valdorda said. “Maybe some horribly dangerous key generation interface has a ‘size’ parameter and they set it to 1 by mistake???”Ben Cartwright-Cox, director of BGP.tools, said: “My guess is that it’s example code that accidentally leaked to production, but hard to know. But it’s bonkers that no one noticed.”At this early stage, the most immediate threat appears to be for those using VPNs, especially in countries with governments likely to maliciously intercept traffic. There are likely many other cases for concern. End users largely have no recourse other than to hold off using many non-browser forms of TLS communication until they receive assurances updates are in place.The whole certificate regime has long been a mess:The incident is the latest to expose a fatal flaw in the TLS regimen. It’s only as strong as its weakest link, which in this case was eMudhra. Fortunately, transparency logs account for much of that failure, but this measure requires parties to actively monitor massive feeds and works only after unauthorized certificates have been issued. eMudhra representatives weren’t immediately available to answer questions.One caveat: exploiting compromised certificates requires an active adversary-in-the-middle attack, meaning the attacker must act as a proxy between two TLS parties and receive encrypted traffic, decrypt it, reencrypt it, and send it to the other party. Such capabilities, in some cases, are usually limited to only the most well-resourced attackers. People with control of a local network­at a coffee shop, university, or other organization­face much less of a challenge.Cleanup of this is going to be another mess—and it’s right on top of the PHP vulnerabilities.

item.title: New Serious PHP Vulnerabilities Released and Patched
item.author: Bruce Schneier
item.content:encoded: PHP maintainers have released fixes for two critical vulnerabilities:PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35 fix two critical vulnerabilities that can allow unauthenticated remote code execution. All PHP users are strongly encouraged to update immediately. Who is at risk: all PHP installations serving web requests, including PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed. We consider the risk highest for mod_php, with a demonstrated exploit where an unauthenticated request can trigger the attack before any application code runs.RCE via OOM corruption, CVE-2026-109618 (GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w): out-of-memory handling can interrupt PHP while internal request data is only partially initialized. Request cleanup may then treat the invalid data as valid. RCE via stale global state, CVE-2026-109619 (GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp): request-owned internal state can survive after its backing memory has been freed. A later request handled by the same worker may use that stale state before normal initialization resets it.Updating PHP is the only way to regain security. Do it now.

item.title: Siemens SIMATIC S7 Webserver API
item.author: CISA
item.content:encoded: .NET Client Library for SIMATIC S7 Webserver API contains multiple vulnerabilities that could allow an attacker to obtain sensitive information or write arbitrary files outside the intended download directory. Siemens has released a new version for .NET Client Library for SIMATIC S7 Webserver API and recommends to update to the latest version.The following versions of Siemens SIMATIC S7 Webserver API are affected:.NET Client Library for SIMATIC S7 Webserver API vers:intdot/<3.3.61, vers:intdot/<3.3.62 (CVE-2026-85114, CVE-2026-85115).NET Client Library for SIMATIC S7 Webserver APIImproper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory ('Path Traversal'), Generation of Error Message Containing Sensitive InformationCritical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical Manufacturing, Transportation Systems, Energy, Healthcare and Public Health, Financial Services, Government Services and FacilitiesCountries/Areas Deployed: WorldwideCompany Headquarters Location: GermanyAffected applications do not properly validate filenames received from remote servers during ticket downloads. This could allow an attacker who can manipulate the ticket response to write arbitrary files outside the intended download directory and, when overwriting is enabled, replace existing files accessible to the application..NET Client Library for SIMATIC S7 Webserver API < V3.3.61Product Status: known_affectedUpdate to V3.3.61 or later versionAffected applications do not properly redact PLC restore passwords from HTTP error exception messages. This could allow an attacker with access to logs or other diagnostic output to obtain the plaintext restore password and potentially perform unauthorized operations on the PLC..NET Client Library for SIMATIC S7 Webserver API < V3.3.61Product Status: known_affected.NET Client Library for SIMATIC S7 Webserver API < V3.3.62Product Status: known_affectedUpdate to V3.3.62 or later versionSiemens ProductCERT reported these vulnerabilities to CISA.As a general security measure, Siemens strongly recommends to protect network access to devices with appropriate mechanisms. In order to operate the devices in a protected IT environment, Siemens recommends to configure the environment according to Siemens' operational guidelines for Industrial Security (Download: https://www.siemens.com/cert/operational-guidelines-industrial-security), and to follow the recommendations in the product manuals. Additional information on Industrial Security by Siemens can be found at: https://www.siemens.com/industrialsecurityFor further inquiries on security vulnerabilities in Siemens products and solutions, please contact the Siemens ProductCERT: https://www.siemens.com/cert/advisoriesThe use of Siemens Security Advisories is subject to the terms and conditions listed on: https://www.siemens.com/productcert/terms-of-use.CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities.Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks.When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices.CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures.Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents.Advisory Conversion DisclaimerThis ICSA is a verbatim republication of Siemens ProductCERT SSA-390352 from a direct conversion of the vendor's Common Security Advisory Framework (CSAF) advisory. This is republished to CISA's website as a means of increasing visibility and is provided "as-is" for informational purposes only. CISA is not responsible for the editorial or technical accuracy of republished advisories and provides no warranties of any kind regarding any information contained within this advisory. Further, CISA does not endorse any commercial product or service. Please contact Siemens ProductCERT directly for any questions regarding this advisory.2026-10-13Initial CISA Republication of Siemens ProductCERT SSA-390352 advisoryLegal Notice and Terms of Use

Healthcare and Public Health, Financial Services, Government Services and FacilitiesCountries/Areas Deployed: WorldwideCompany Headquarters Location: Germanysshd in OpenSSH 6.2 through 8.x before 8.8, when certain non-default configurations are used, allows privilege escalation because supplemental groups are not initialized as expected. Helper programs for AuthorizedKeysCommand and AuthorizedPrincipalsCommand may run with privileges associated with group memberships of the sshd process, if the configuration specifies running the risk of this vulnerability.Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, and ensure they are not accessible from the internet.Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolate them from business networks.When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most recent version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as its connected devices.CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures.CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies.CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets. Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies.Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents.Advisory Conversion DisclaimerThis ICSA is a verbatim republication of Siemens ProductCERT SSA-457936 from a direct conversion of the vendor's Common Security Advisory Framework (CSAF) advisory. item.title: Siemens SIMATIC S7-1500 TM MFP
item.author: CISA
item.content:encoded: Multiple vulnerabilities have been identified in the additional GNU/Linux subsystem of the SIMATIC S7-1500 TM MFP V1.1.1. Siemens is preparing fixes and recommends specific mitigations for products where fixes are not or not yet available.The following versions of Siemens SIMATIC S7-1500 TM MFP are affected:SIMATIC S7-1500 TM MFP - GNU/Linux subsystem vers:all/* SIMATIC S7-1500 TM MFP - GNU/Linux subsystemAccess of Uninitialized Pointer, Buffer Copy without Checking Size of Input ('Classic Buffer Overflow'), Deadlock, Detection of Error Condition Without Action, Double Free, Expired Pointer Dereference, Heap-based Buffer Overflow, Improper Control of Resource Identifiers ('Resource Injection'), Improper Control of a Resource Through its Lifetime, Improper Handling of Length Parameter Inconsistency, Improper Handling of Missing Special Element, Improper Handling of Structural Elements, Improper Input Validation, Improper Locking, Improper Resource Locking, Improper Restriction of Operations within the Bounds of a Memory Buffer, Improper Update of Reference Count, Improper Validation of Array Index, Improper Validation of Consistency within Input, Improper Validation of Specified Index, Position, or Offset in Input, Improper Validation of Specified Quantity in Input, Improper Validation of Specified Type of Input, Incorrect Synchronization, Integer Overflow or Wraparound, Integer Underflow (Wrap or Wraparound), Loop with Unreachable Exit Condition ('Infinite Loop'), Missing Default Case in Multiple Condition Expression, Missing Initialization of Resource, Missing Lock Check, Missing Release of Memory after Effective Lifetime, Missing Release of Resource after Effective Lifetime, Multiple Locks of a Critical Resource, NULL Pointer Dereference, Operation on a Resource after Expiration or Release, Out-of-bounds Read, Out-of-bounds Write, Plaintext Storage of a Password, Release of Invalid Pointer or Reference, Return of Wrong Status Code, Signal Handler Race Condition, Time-of-check Time-of-use (TOCTOU) Race Condition, Unchecked Return Value, Use After Free, Use of Incorrect Operator, Use of Uninitialized Resource, Write-what-where ConditionCritical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical Manufacturing, Transportation Systems, Energy, Healthcare and Public Health, Financial Services, Government Services and FacilitiesCountries/Areas Deployed: WorldwideCompany Headquarters Location: GermanyIn the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: netfilter: allow exp not to be removed in nf_ct_find_expectation Currently nf_conntrack_in() calling nf_ct_find_expectation() will remove the exp from the hash table. However, in some scenario, we expect the exp not to be removed when the created ct will not be confirmed, like in OVS and TC conntrack in the following patches. This patch allows exp not to be removed by setting IPS_CONFIRMED in the status of the tmpl.SIMATIC S7-1500 TM MFP - GNU/Linux subsystemProduct Status: known_affectedLimit access to the interactive shell of the additional GNU/Linux subssytem to trusted personnel only.Only build and run applications from trusted sources.Currently no fix is availableSiemens ProductCERT reported these vulnerabilities to CISA.As a general security measure, Siemens strongly recommends to protect network access to devices with appropriate mechanisms. In order to operate the devices in a protected IT environment, Siemens recommends to configure the environment according to Siemens' operational guidelines for Industrial Security (Download: https://www.siemens.com/cert/operational-guidelines-industrial-security), and to follow the recommendations in the product manuals. Additional information on Industrial Security by Siemens can be found at: https://www.siemens.com/industrialsecurityFor further inquiries on security vulnerabilities in Siemens products and solutions, please contact the Siemens ProductCERT: https://www.siemens.com/cert/advisoriesThe use of Siemens Security Advisories is subject to the terms and conditions listed on: https://www.siemens.com/productcert/terms-of-use.CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities.Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks.When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices.CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures.Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents.Advisory Conversion DisclaimerThis ICSA is a verbatim republication of Siemens ProductCERT SSA-784472 from a direct conversion of the vendor's Common Security Advisory Framework (CSAF) advisory. This is republished to CISA's website as a means of increasing visibility and is provided "as-is" for informational purposes only. item.title: Siemens RUGGEDCOM APE1808 Devices
item.author: CISA
item.content:encoded: Nozomi Networks has published information on vulnerabilities in Nozomi Guardian/CMC. This advisory lists the related Siemens Industrial products affected by these vulnerabilities. Siemens recommends to contact customer support to receive patch and update information.The following versions of Siemens RUGGEDCOM APE1808 Devices are affected:RUGGEDCOM APE1808 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-33387, CVE-2026-33388, CVE-2026-33389, CVE-2026-33391, CVE-2026-33920)Improper Neutralization of Special Elements Used in a Template Engine, Incorrect Authorization, Lack of Administrator Control over Security, Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical Manufacturing, Transportation Systems, Energy, Healthcare and Public Health, Financial Services, Government Services and FacilitiesCountries/Areas Deployed: WorldwideCompany Headquarters Location: GermanyA template injection vulnerability was discovered in the Dashboards functionality due to improper validation of an input parameter. An authenticated user with the required privileges can define a dashboard containing a malicious payload, or a victim can be socially engineered into importing a malicious dashboard. When the victim views or imports the dashboard, the payload executes in their browser context, allowing the attacker to modify application data or disrupt application availability.RUGGEDCOM APE1808 with Nozomi Guardian/CMCProduct Status: known_affectedContact customer support to receive patch and update informationAn access control vulnerability was discovered in the Credentials Manager functionality due to insufficient validation of user privileges. A remote authenticated user with limited privileges can view a limited subset of the available entries in the Credentials Manager. The actual credential values are not directly visible, but the user can delete entries or edit their properties. An attacker who deletes or edits an entry can disrupt authentication for dependent devices, and one who manipulates an entry's configuration may be able to indirectly obtain the credentials.RUGGEDCOM APE1808 with Nozomi Guardian/CMCProduct Status: known_affectedContact customer support to receive patch and update informationRUGGEDCOM APE1808 with Nozomi Guardian/CMCProduct Status: known_affectedContact customer support to receive patch and update informationAn improper certificate/host key validation vulnerability was discovered in the Smart Polling functionality, which established encrypted connections to target devices without validating the remote host's identity, and no option was provided to enable it. A man-in-the-middle attacker positioned between a sensor and a polled device can, during a polling session, impersonate the device and intercept the communication, including the credentials used to access it. The captured credentials can then be replayed to authenticate against the device itself or against other devices sharing the same credentials, allowing the attacker to access and tamper with the device's data and to disrupt its operations.RUGGEDCOM APE1808 with Nozomi Guardian/CMCProduct Status: known_affectedContact customer support to receive patch and update informationRUGGEDCOM APE1808 with Nozomi Guardian/CMCProduct Status: known_affectedContact customer support to receive patch and update informationRUGGEDCOM APE1808 with Nozomi Guardian/CMCProduct Status: known_affectedContact customer support to receive patch and update informationAn access control vulnerability was discovered in the Smart Polling configuration functionality due to insufficient validation of user privileges. An authenticated user with limited privileges can remotely bypass the intended access control of the web management interface and modify the Smart Polling discovery configuration. This allows the attacker to disrupt the visibility of assets in the monitored network.RUGGEDCOM APE1808 with Nozomi Guardian/CMCProduct Status: known_affectedContact customer support to receive patch and update informationRUGGEDCOM APE1808 with Nozomi Guardian/CMCProduct Status: known_affectedContact customer support to receive patch and update informationRUGGEDCOM APE1808 with Nozomi Guardian/CMCProduct Status: known_affectedContact customer support to receive patch and update informationRUGGEDCOM APE1808 with Nozomi Guardian/CMCProduct Status: known_affectedContact customer support to receive patch and update informationA cross-site request forgery vulnerability was discovered in the login functionality (both standard and SAML) due to missing validation of the anti-CSRF token. An attacker with a valid account can trick a victim into unknowingly authenticating with the attacker's credentials. Any operation performed by the victim in this state is attributed to the attacker's account, compromising the integrity of the audit trail.RUGGEDCOM APE1808 with Nozomi Guardian/CMCProduct Status: known_affectedContact customer support to receive patch and update informationRUGGEDCOM APE1808 with Nozomi Guardian/CMCProduct Status: known_affectedContact customer support to receive patch and update informationRUGGEDCOM APE1808 with Nozomi Guardian/CMCProduct Status: known_affectedContact customer support to receive patch and update informationRUGGEDCOM APE1808 with Nozomi Guardian/CMCProduct Status: known_affectedContact customer support to receive patch and update informationRUGGEDCOM APE1808 with Nozomi Guardian/CMCProduct Status: known_affectedContact customer support to receive patch and update informationSiemens ProductCERT reported these vulnerabilities to CISA.As a general security measure, Siemens strongly recommends to protect network access to devices with appropriate mechanisms. In order to operate the devices in a protected IT environment, Siemens recommends to configure the environment according to Siemens' operational guidelines for Industrial Security (Download: https://www.siemens.com/cert/operational-guidelines-industrial-security), and to follow the recommendations in the product manuals. Additional information on Industrial Security by Siemens can be found at: https://www.siemens.com/industrialsecurityFor further inquiries on security vulnerabilities in Siemens products and solutions, please contact the Siemens ProductCERT: https://www.siemens.com/cert/advisoriesThe use of Siemens Security Advisories is subject to the terms and conditions listed on: https://www.siemens.com/productcert/terms-of-use.CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities.Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks.When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices.CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures.Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents.Advisory Conversion DisclaimerThis ICSA is a verbatim republication of Siemens ProductCERT SSA-911336 from a direct conversion of the vendor's Common Security Advisory Framework (CSAF) advisory. This is republished to CISA's website as a means of increasing visibility and is provided "as-is" for informational purposes only. CISA is not responsible for the editorial or technical accuracy of republished advisories and provides no warranties of any kind regarding any information contained within this advisory. Further, CISA does not endorse any commercial product or service. Please contact Siemens ProductCERT directly for any questions regarding this advisory.2026-10-13Initial CISA Republication of Siemens ProductCERT SSA-911336 advisoryLegal Notice and Terms of Use

item.title: Siemens RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW Station Access Controller
item.author: CISA
item.content:encoded: RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW Station Access Controller (SAC) contains multiple vulnerabilities in the integrated SQLite component that could allow an attacker to execute arbitrary code, cause a denial of service, or obtain sensitive information. Siemens has released a new version for RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW Station Access Controller (SAC) and recommends to update to the latest version.The following versions of Siemens RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW Station Access Controller are affected:RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW Station Access Controller (SAC) vers:intdot/<6.0 (CVE-2025-6965, CVE-2025-70873, CVE-2025-71316, CVE-2026-11822, CVE-2026-11824)RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW Station Access Controller (SAC)Numeric Truncation Error, Improper Clearing of Heap Memory Before Release ('Heap Inspection'), Improper Handling of Unicode Encoding, Heap-based Buffer OverflowCritical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical Manufacturing, Transportation Systems, Energy, Healthcare and Public Health, Financial Services, Government Services and FacilitiesCountries/Areas Deployed: WorldwideCompany Headquarters Location: GermanyThere exists a vulnerability in SQLite versions before 3.50.2 where the number of aggregate terms could exceed the number of columns available. This could lead to a memory corruption issue. We recommend upgrading to version 3.50.2 or above.RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW Station Access Controller (SAC) < V6.0Product Status: known_affectedUpdate to V6.0 or later versionAn information disclosure issue in the zipfileInflate function in the zipfile extension in SQLite v3.51.1 and earlier allows attackers to obtain heap memory via supplying a crafted ZIP file.RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW Station Access Controller (SAC) < V6.0Product Status: known_affectedUpdate to V6.0 or later versionRUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW Station Access Controller (SAC) < V6.0Product Status: known_affectedUpdate to V6.0 or later versionSQLite 'sqldiff.exe' does not securely handle the way the Microsoft Windows C runtime converts Unicode characters to ANSI codepages. An attacker could use the '-L' option to load an arbitrary DLL with a crafted command line argument string that results in command line file arguments being misinterpreted as command line options. Fixed on or around 2025-12-26.RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW Station Access Controller (SAC) < V6.0Product Status: known_affectedUpdate to V6.0 or later versionRUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW Station Access Controller (SAC) < V6.0Product Status: known_affectedUpdate to V6.0 or later versionRUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW Station Access Controller (SAC) < V6.0Product Status: known_affectedUpdate to V6.0 or later versionSQLite before 3.53.2 contains memory corruption vulnerabilities in the FTS5 full-text search extension that allow attackers to cause process crashes, memory exhaustion, or arbitrary code execution by supplying a crafted database with malformed FTS5 page data. Attackers can trigger an out-of-bounds read in fts5LeafSeek() via an attacker-controlled loop bound and a heap buffer overflow write in fts5ChunkIterate() through a crafted continuation page causing an integer underflow, exploitable when an FTS5 MATCH query is executed against the malicious database.RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW Station Access Controller (SAC) < V6.0Product Status: known_affectedUpdate to V6.0 or later versionRUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW Station Access Controller (SAC) < V6.0Product Status: known_affectedUpdate to V6.0 or later versionRUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW Station Access Controller (SAC) < V6.0Product Status: known_affectedUpdate to V6.0 or later versionRUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW Station Access Controller (SAC) < V6.0Product Status: known_affectedUpdate to V6.0 or later versionSQLite before 3.53.2 contains a heap-based buffer overflow vulnerability in the FTS5 full-text search extension that allows attackers to cause a crash or execute arbitrary code by supplying a crafted database with malicious continuation page metadata specifying a szLeaf value smaller than 4. Attackers can trigger an integer underflow in fts5ChunkIterate() causing an inflated remaining byte count during FTS5 MATCH query processing, leading to a heap buffer overflow of attacker-controlled data in applications compiled with SQLITE_ENABLE_FTS5.RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW Station Access Controller (SAC) < V6.0Product Status: known_affectedUpdate to V6.0 or later versionRUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW Station Access Controller (SAC) < V6.0Product Status: known_affectedUpdate to V6.0 or later versionRUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW Station Access Controller (SAC) < V6.0Product Status: known_affectedUpdate to V6.0 or later versionRUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW Station Access Controller (SAC) < V6.0Product Status: known_affectedUpdate to V6.0 or later versionRUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW Station Access Controller (SAC) < V6.0Product Status: known_affectedUpdate to V6.0 or later versionSiemens ProductCERT reported these vulnerabilities to CISA.As a general security measure, Siemens strongly recommends to protect network access to devices with appropriate mechanisms. In order to operate the devices in a protected IT environment, Siemens recommends to configure the environment according to Siemens' operational guidelines for Industrial Security (Download: https://www.siemens.com/cert/operational-guidelines-industrial-security), and to follow the recommendations in the product manuals. Additional information on Industrial Security by Siemens can be found at: https://www.siemens.com/industrialsecurityFor further inquiries on security vulnerabilities in Siemens products and solutions, please contact the Siemens ProductCERT: https://www.siemens.com/cert/advisoriesThe use of Siemens Security Advisories is subject to the terms and conditions listed on: https://www.siemens.com/productcert/terms-of-use.CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities.Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks.When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices.CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures.Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents.Advisory Conversion DisclaimerThis ICSA is a verbatim republication of Siemens ProductCERT SSA-765416 from a direct conversion of the vendor's Common Security Advisory Framework (CSAF) advisory. This is republished to CISA's website as a means of increasing visibility and is provided "as-is" for informational purposes only. CISA is not responsible for the editorial or technical accuracy of republished advisories and provides no warranties of any kind regarding any information contained within this advisory. Further, CISA does not endorse any commercial product or service. Please contact Siemens ProductCERT directly for any questions regarding this advisory.2026-10-13Initial CISA Republication of Siemens ProductCERT SSA-765416 advisoryLegal Notice and Terms of Use
